reason: All 30 blocks are the same connectivity (C7H15NO): an aziridine N (pyramidal tertiary amine, N bonded to the stereocenter C6 and to the two ring CH2 carbons C8/C9 which are mutually bonded, C8-C9 ~1.48 A confirming the 3-membered ring), with C6 bearing an n-propyl chain (C3-C2-C1), a CH2OH arm (C14-O15-H16), and H. The aziridine ring strain is constant across conformers, so relative stability is governed mainly by (a) an intramolecular O-H...N hydrogen bond, (b) N-inversion/lone-pair orientation that enables it, and (c) gauche/steric folding of the propyl chain against the aziridine/CH2OH. I therefore estimated O...N and H(O)...N distances for every conformer. A clear bimodal pattern appears: eight structures have O...N ~3.67-3.68 A (OH rotated anti, no H-bond: 4,12,13,15,18,22,23,29) and are intrinsically less stable; the other 22 have O...N ~2.72-2.97 A with an H-bond of varying strength. Ranking the H-bonded set primarily by H...N shortness (and O...N/linearity): 28 (2.17/2.72) is best; 25,11,26,6 (~2.22-2.23/2.74-2.75) form the next tight cluster (ordering among them is uncertain and depends on lone-pair alignment and minor chain gauche); 24 (2.30/2.80), 3 and 19 (2.27/2.78), 17,20,21 (2.29/2.79) are good-moderate; 2,14,27 (2.35-2.36/2.83-2.84) moderate; 8,5,9,10,7,30,1,16 are progressively weaker (H...N 2.51-2.64, O...N up to 2.97), the last of these barely better than no H-bond. Within the non-H-bonded group I ordered by apparent chain extension (more anti/extended propyl = less 1,3 steric and fewer eclipsing contacts) placing 15,29,4,18 above 22,13,23, with 12 the most folded/compact and hence least stable. Major uncertainties: exact N lone-pair direction (inversion) cannot be read from coordinates alone, and the energy gaps within each cluster are small (likely <1-2 kcal/mol), so adjacent swaps are plausible; the big gap is between the 22 H-bonded and the 8 non-H-bonded conformers.

The molecule is C5H9N3O = CH3CH2-NH-CH(CN)-C(=O)NH2: a chiral alpha-carbon bearing H, an ethylamino group (secondary amine N3-H, donor/acceptor), a linear nitrile (C6≡N7, acceptor only) and a planar carboxamide (C9=O10, N11H2 donor; O10 is the best acceptor). Conformers differ mainly by rotation about N3-C5 and C5-C9, so the dominant discriminator is whether a 5-membered intramolecular H-bond closes across N3-C5-C9: either (A) amine N3-H...O10=C, heavy-atom N3...O10 ≈ 2.7-2.8 Å, or (B) amide N11-H...N3, N3...N11 ≈ 2.7-3.0 Å. Type A uses the stronger donor (amine NH) and the best acceptor (carbonyl O), so it is favored over type B (amide NH is a weaker donor, amine N only a moderate acceptor). Repulsion between the two negative termini (carbonyl O10 and nitrile N7) is relieved in all conformers (O10...N7 ≈ 3.6-4.5 Å), so it does not separate them. I estimated N3...O10, N3...N11 and O10...N7 for every conformer. Clean type-A H-bonds (N3...O10 ≈ 2.71-2.78) occur in 6,14,17,9,8,10,30,1,15,5,16,22 and these are ranked highest, ordered roughly by H-bond distance (2.71-2.73 before 2.76-2.78); differences among them are within geometric noise and are the main uncertainty. Type-B H-bonds follow: the most ideal-distance ones 28(≈3.02) and 24(≈2.98), then 4,12,18,25(≈2.69), 2(2.75),23(2.70),27(2.67). The conformers whose only contact is a compressed N3...N11 ≈ 2.62-2.66 (11,13,19,29,20,3,26) suffer N...N compression/strain with only a bent, partial H-bond, so they fall lower, the most compressed (≈2.62: 20,3,26) lowest of that set. Conformers 21 and 7 have both N3...O10 and N3...N11 ≈ 3.15-3.2 Å, i.e. no real intramolecular H-bond (extended), so despite being torsionally relaxed they lack internal stabilization and are placed last; ordering within each tier is uncertain because I could not resolve small torsional/eth­yl-gauche differences or exact H-bond linearity from coordinates alone.

The atom order corresponds to ethyl 2-aminopropanoate, CH3-CH2-O-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-NH2. The ester C2-O5-C6-O7 unit remains close to the usual planar Z arrangement in all 30 structures, so the principal discriminators are the C1-C2-O5-C6 ethyl torsion, rotation about C6-C8, the orientation of NH2 toward the two ester oxygens, and methyl-oxygen crowding. Structures with C1...C6 near 3.58-3.64 A and C1...O7 near 4.1 A have the ethyl tail anti; those with C1...C6 near 3.12-3.15 A and C1...O7 near 3.22-3.26 A are gauche and are modestly more crowded. Conformers 25, 2, 1, 27, 13, and 30 form the most favorable backbone motif: N9...O7 is about 2.78 A and one N-H is only 2.35-2.38 A from the carbonyl oxygen, giving a bent five-member N-H...O=C contact. The anti members 27, 30, 13, and 25 are placed before gauche 2 and 1; their mutual order is nearly degenerate, with 27 and 30 having slightly better combinations of donor distance and methyl/ethyl clearance. Conformers 16, 18, 5, 26, 12, and 3 also place N near the carbonyl oxygen, but the shortest N-H...O=C distances are around 2.60-2.62 A and the alpha methyl is only about 2.96-2.98 A from the alkoxy oxygen, so this is a weaker and more crowded motif. Anti 12, 26, 5, and 16 precede gauche 3 and 18. Conformers 29, 6, and 15 have a short N-H...O contact of about 2.35-2.36 A, but the acceptor is the less basic ester alkoxy oxygen and C12 is also about 3.04-3.06 A from that oxygen. Anti 29 and 6 therefore follow the carbonyl-bound group; gauche 15 remains competitive because of its short donor contact. Conformers 20, 10, 14, 9, 11, 8, and 19 are anti but have tighter N...O(alkoxy) contacts, approximately 2.66-2.68 A, with N-H...O around 2.46-2.50 A. They are ordered mainly by balancing N-O crowding against the exact donor distance and the roughly 3.05-3.08 A methyl-oxygen contacts. Among the gauche alkoxy-bound structures, 4 is favored because its methyl group is unusually clear of both oxygens, followed by 22 and 7, which have comparatively good donor distances and methyl clearance. Conformer 24 is less favorable because both N and the alpha methyl approach the same ester oxygen. Conformers 21 and 28 avoid very short N-O contacts but pay for this with a direct C12...O7 contact of only about 2.80-2.82 A; 21 is preferred because its N-H...O contact is shorter and its methyl-carbonyl contact is slightly longer. Conformers 23, 17, and especially 28 occupy the bottom because they combine gauche ethyl strain with either a very short N-O contact or the severe alpha-methyl/carbonyl-oxygen clash. Differences within the four strongest anti conformers and within the anti alkoxy-bound block are small, likely only a few tenths of a kcal/mol, and the positions of 15 relative to the anti alkoxy group and of 21 relative to 23/17 are particularly uncertain without electronic energies, entropy, or solvation.

I treated the labels as arbitrary and ignored block order. The common framework is CH3-C≡C-CH2-O-CH2-CH(OH)-CH3, so the main discriminators are: (1) whether the terminal OH can donate an intramolecular H bond to the ether O, judged by Oether...Ohydroxyl near 2.7-2.9 A, H...Oether roughly 2.1-2.4 A, and an O-H...O angle that is not bent away; (2) whether the two methyl/alkyne termini are extended rather than folded into each other; (3) whether an O...O contact is short while the OH points away, which is worse than no contact because it gives lone-pair/O-O repulsion without H-bond payoff; (4) obvious eclipsing/compactness in the C-O-C-C and C-C-O-C torsions. Strong H-bonded and still relatively extended conformers look best: 4 and 28 have short H...Oether contacts near 2.2 A with favorable angles and separated ends; 3 and 14 combine good H-bond geometry with very large methyl-to-methyl separation; 29, 7, 9, 22, 8, 5, 19 and 15 also show credible O-H...Oether bonds, with 19/15 somewhat more compact and 5 more folded despite a good local H bond. A middle group is extended but lacks a real H bond: 23, 24, 1, 10, 11, 27, 2, 21, 16, 26 and 13 are mostly anti/extended enough to avoid severe methyl clashes, but the OH is unsatisfied or pointing away. Conformers 6, 18, 25 and 20 are penalized because Oether...Ohydroxyl is fairly short yet the hydroxyl H is poorly aligned, suggesting repulsive O...O proximity rather than stabilization. The least stable are compact/non-H-bonded structures: 17 and 30 fold the termini without an H-bond payoff, and 12 is especially unfavorable because it is compact with a short-ish O...O separation but bad OH orientation, giving steric plus electrostatic strain. The ranking is uncertain within the strong-H-bond group because small changes in torsion angle or H position could reorder 3/4/7/14/28/29, and the extended no-H-bond group is also close; the clearest separation is strong aligned H bond > extended non-H-bonded > short but misaligned O...O > compact non-H-bonded.

The common skeleton contains a rigid cyclopropane ring bearing one hydroxyl and an adjacent secondary-alcohol side chain with an isopropyl group. Ring bond lengths and angles are similar throughout, so the ranking is governed mainly by two staggered rotamers, hydroxyl orientation, and nonbonded contacts rather than by differences in cyclopropane strain. I first examined the two alcohol oxygens. Conformer 28 has the clearest intramolecular O-H···O interaction: O···O about 2.66 A and H···O about 2.04 A with an O-H···O angle near 120 degrees. Conformers 19 and 11 also have compressed O···O distances, about 2.73 and 2.72 A, with H···O near 2.14-2.15 A and angles around 117-119 degrees. Conformer 22 has a shorter O···O separation of about 2.70 A, but its roughly 111-degree donor angle makes the interaction substantially weaker. Several other structures have short H···O distances, but angles near 90-110 degrees make them poor hydrogen bonds. Around the isopropyl-carbinol bond, the least crowded staggered family places the two methyl groups approximately anti to the cyclopropyl and hydroxyl substituents and places the two methine hydrogens anti to one another; this family comprises 7, 12, 13, 15, 21, 24, 25, 26, 27, and 29. Within it, 13, 7, 12, 27, 25, and 15 also separate the two alcohol oxygens to roughly 3.54-3.64 A while keeping the isopropyl side chain about 3.17-3.32 A from the ring hydroxyl. Their relative order follows the remaining methine-H/oxygen and methyl contacts, with 15 penalized by a particularly short ring-O to methine-H contact near 2.34 A. Conformer 8 has a favorable side-chain to ring-OH separation near 3.23 A and gauche alcohols, but it lacks a well-directed O-H···O bond and uses a more crowded backbone rotamer. Conformers 21, 24, 26, and 29 retain the favorable central methyl arrangement, yet their cyclopropyl-OH is only about 2.87-2.96 A from the isopropyl-bearing carbon while the second oxygen is also gauche, giving a compact, more crowded region. The next group, 2, 20, 1, 3, 5, 9, and 14, combines gauche alcohols with progressively worse central-rotamer contacts, including several methine H···H or methyl H···methine H separations near 2.33-2.55 A; 2 and 1 receive small offsets from very bent O-H···O approaches, while 14 and 9 have the shortest H···H contacts. The least stable structures, 16, 30, 10, 18, 23, 17, 6, and 4, either place the isopropyl side chain only about 2.85-2.96 A from the cyclopropanol oxygen without a compensating hydroxyl hydrogen bond or combine that contact with an unfavorable methyl/hydrogen rotamer. Conformers 6 and 4 are lowest because the side-chain/ring-OH distance is only about 2.85 A in addition to several 2.4-2.7 A hydrogen contacts. The largest uncertainty is in the middle, especially among 7, 12, 13, 15, 25, 27 and 8, 21, 24, 26, 29, where the balance between anti dipole/oxygen separation and backbone sterics is subtle; several adjacent pairs could interchange under a full force-field optimization.

I treated the connectivity as fixed: an ethyl group (C1-C2), a central CH (C5), an N-aziridine substituent (N6-C7-C8), and a methoxymethyl group (C13-O14-C15). Because there are no O-H or N-H donors, I did not look for classical hydrogen bonds; the main geometry terms are staggered vs gauche/eclipsed relationships about C2-C5, C5-N6, C5-C13 and C13-O14, avoidance of methyl/ring close contacts, and N...O lone-pair/dipole proximity. The three-membered aziridine strain is essentially common to all, so I used it only to say that orientations forcing the ring toward the ethyl or methoxymethyl groups are worse. I estimated which rotamer each coordinate set represents from distances such as C1...N6/C1...C13 (ethyl methyl anti to aziridine or to CH2OMe), C1...C15 (terminal methyl-methyl separation), and N6...O14 (large separation preferred because both are acceptors). Balanced conformers with the ethyl methyl directed away from the rigid aziridine, terminal methyls well separated, and N/O not folded together were ranked highest: 14, 12, 21, 6, 1, 20 and 30 fit this best, with 12/5/23 slightly penalized for N...O being near 3 A and 21/6 for only moderate C1...C15 separation. Structures with very large C1...C15 but short C1...N6 or borderline N...O contacts (26, 13, 16, 28, 29, 3) are good but less balanced. Conformers 24, 19, 8 and 11 have the ethyl/ring relationship acceptable but show more compact terminal-group packing. The lowest group (4, 25, 15, 2, 17, 18) places C1 gauche to both the aziridine and methoxymethyl substituents rather than cleanly anti to either; 18 is worst because it also has the shortest terminal methyl-methyl separation and a folded N/O arrangement. Differences in the middle are small and uncertain, roughly at the few-kcal rotamer level rather than an exact energy ordering.

The molecule is C7H16O2, a 3-methylhexane-1,4-diol skeleton (same atom order in every block: atom 9 = secondary C4-OH oxygen with H10, atom 19 = primary C1-OH oxygen with H20; C12 is the methyl-bearing stereocenter). The dominant energetic discriminator is therefore an intramolecular O-H···O hydrogen bond closing a pseudo-7-membered ring (O9-C8-C12-C17-C18-O19). I scored each conformer by (i) O9···O19 distance, (ii) donor-H···acceptor-O distance, (iii) O-H···O angle, and (iv) secondary steric strain (folding required for the H-bond vs. methyl/chain gauche crowding and H···H contacts).

Clear, strong, near-linear H-bonds (O···O ≈ 2.73-2.87 Å, H···O ≈ 1.82-1.96 Å, angle ≈ 149-159°) are present in 18 conformers: 13 (primary→secondary, 2.75 Å/1.82/158°), 8 (2.745/1.815/159°), 30 (2.731/1.822/155°), 1 (2.735/1.819/156°), 27 (2.78/1.857/158°), 11 (2.78/1.859/157°), 10 (2.80/1.874/158°), 16 (2.757/1.847/154°), 23 (2.762/1.855/154°), 19 (2.859/1.955/154°), 5 (2.814/1.914/153°), 6 (2.82/1.92/153°), 20 (2.739/1.856/150°), 12 (2.843/1.949/152°), 25 (2.87/1.975/152°), 18 (2.735/1.851/149°), 28 (2.735/1.855/149°), 22 (2.816/1.966/145°). These form the stable upper block; I ordered them by combined shortness of O···O and linearity of the O-H···O angle (8, 13, 30, 1, 27, 11, 10 best; 28, 22 least linear within the block).

A marginal group has O···O ≈ 2.85-2.99 Å but poor donation: 17 (2.99 Å, H···O 2.27, angle 131° — a real but bent weak bond, best of this set), 26 (2.89 Å but both donor H ≈ 2.4-2.5 Å, no good geometry), 21 (2.88 Å, angle ≈111°, too bent), 24 (2.90 Å, H ≈2.4, angle ≈112°). These get only weak electrostatic benefit.

No H-bond (O···O > 3.6 Å): 9 (4.90), 14 (5.23), 29 (4.96), 2 (5.22) are extended and relatively unstrained but forfeit the H-bond; 4 (3.62), 3 (3.87), 7 (3.90), 15 (3.93) are folded/compact yet still fail to engage the second OH, so they pay gauche/steric cost without the H-bond payoff and are the least stable (15 and 7 are the most O-O-separated of the folded non-bonded set). The boundary between the weak-bent H-bond group and the extended non-H-bond group is the main uncertainty (roughly a 1-3 kcal/mol trade-off), as is the fine order inside the large strong-H-bond block where several geometries are nearly isoenergetic.

I treated the connectivity as CH3-CO-CH2-C7(OH)-C8H2-C9H(OH) cyclopropane: O3 is the ketone acceptor, O15 is the tertiary cyclopropanol on C7, and O10 is the secondary alcohol on C9. In nearly every geometry the two alcohol O atoms are >3.5 A apart, so OH...OH bonding is not a major discriminator; the dominant stabilizing term is an intramolecular O-H...O3=C contact. I compared donor H...O3 distance, O...O distance, approximate O-H...O angle, and the pseudo-ring size: O15-H...O3 gives a six-membered path, whereas O10-H...O3 gives a seven-membered path but often a more linear contact. The best cases are 26, 15 and 5: O10-H...O3 is short and nearly linear, about 1.87-1.90 A with O...O about 2.80-2.83 A and angle near 157-158 deg; I order them 26 > 15 > 5 mainly by the shortest H...O/O...O contacts, but they are close. 28 and 13 are next: good O10-H...O3 contacts around 1.94-1.99 A, slightly less linear than the top three. 1 has a shorter O15-H...O3 contact, about 1.97 A, and a favorable six-membered closure, but the angle is only ~138 deg, so I place it after the more linear 28/13 and before 21. 21 is a good but longer O10-H...O3 bond (~2.02 A, angle ~141 deg). 29, 3, 11 and 6 form six-membered O15-H...O3 contacts of moderate quality, roughly 2.05-2.12 A and angles ~128-132 deg; I order them mostly by H...O distance/angle as 29 > 3 > 11 > 6, with 3/11 nearly interchangeable. 22 and 12 have only weak/long O10-H...O3 contacts (~2.3 A, angle ~125 deg), so they are clearly below the previous group but still better than geometries with no acceptor contact. 20, 8 and 24 have at most marginal contacts (~2.45-2.50 A, poor angles or long O...O), with 24 penalized for being more compact. The remaining structures have no credible H bond: the more extended ones (14, 23, 18, 25, 16, 27) are placed above compact non-H-bonded forms, while 2, 9, 30, 17, 10, 4, 19 and especially 7 bring the methyl/carbonyl end closer to the cyclopropane/diol end without forming an H bond, suggesting steric/eclipsing penalty and unfavorable dipole/OH orientation. The largest uncertainty is among the extended no-H-bond conformers and among 1 versus 13/21, where six-membered closure competes with better linearity.

The atom ordering is identical in every block (C1 methyl, C3 carbinol, O4 hydroxyl, H5 hydroxyl H, C7 central CH, C8 aldehyde, O9 aldehyde O, C11 ketone, O12 ketone O, C13 methyl), giving C6H10O3: CH3-CH(OH)-CH(CHO)-CO-CH3 (an alpha-formyl beta-hydroxy methyl ketone). The dominant discriminator is an intramolecular O4-H5...O hydrogen bond to one of the two carbonyl acceptors (a pseudo-six-membered ring O4-C3-C7-C(=O)); secondary is O9...O12 separation (anti carbonyls reduce dipole/O...O repulsion) and general folded/steric crowding. I estimated H5...O9/H5...O12, O4...O, and O9...O12 from coordinates. Clear IMHB (H...O ~1.9-2.1 A, O...O ~2.7-2.8 A, near-linear): 20 (to ketone, shortest ~1.93, carbonyls anti ~4.3) strongest; 27 and 8 (to ketone, ~2.0-2.1, angle ~130); 3 (to aldehyde, ~2.0, very linear ~133 and carbonyls very anti ~4.4); 29 (ketone ~2.1); 28 (ketone ~2.17 but O9...O12 only ~3.7, slight carbonyl repulsion). Moderate/bent IMHB (H...O ~2.18-2.24, angle ~124-131): 26 (aldehyde, carbonyls most anti ~4.6), 1 (aldehyde, fairly linear), 19 (aldehyde, anti ~4.4), 13 (aldehyde a bit long but carbonyls ~4.5), then 18 (ketone acceptor but bent ~124) and 15 (bent aldehyde) as the weakest of the H-bonded set; ketone vs aldehyde acceptor strength and the O9...O12 separation make 18/15/13/19 ordering genuinely uncertain. The remaining 18 have H5 pointing away from both carbonyls (H...O >3 A), so no IMHB; among them I favor larger O9...O12 and less folded shapes: 6 (~4.7, most anti) and 30 (~4.3) lead, then a broad, uncertain middle (~3.8-4.1: 22,16,14,12,4,9,7,17,25,5,24,2,11,23), while 21 (~3.5) and 10 (~3.4) have the two C=O groups closest (largest dipole/steric penalty) and are placed last. Uncertainty is high within the no-H-bond middle because eclipsing/gauche penalties around C3-C7 and C7-C11 cannot be fully resolved without dihedrals; the H-bonded vs non-H-bonded split, and the lead of 20, are the robust conclusions.

All 30 blocks share one atom order and one connectivity (C7H11NO): a partially saturated six-membered N-H ring (atoms 5-10) bearing a methyl/short alkyl group at C5-C1 and a -CH2OH arm (C12-O15-H16) on the ring carbon adjacent to N (C9). With no energies given, I compared each geometry on three robust, coordinate-based criteria rather than block order or label size. (1) Intramolecular H-bond: the dominant stabilizer is a folded geometry that brings O15 within ~2.7-3.0 A of the enamine/amine N10 with the O-H (H16) directed toward the N lone pair (O-H...N, ~5-membered pseudo-ring N10-C9-C12-O15-H16), or the reverse N10-H11...O15. I estimated d(N10-O15) and whether H16 (or H11) points inward. (2) Steric congestion: short nonbonded H...H contacts (<~2.1 A) and close approach of the C1 methyl/C5 methylene to the C12H2-O15 arm or to ring C-H hydrogens raise energy; eclipsing about C5-C6 and C9-C12 also costs. (3) Conjugation/ring strain: the N10-C9=C8 and C6=C7 ene/enamine fragments prefer near-planarity; strongly puckered or twisted conformers lose conjugation, while a modest fold that enables the H-bond is worth it. Applying this, conformers 5 and 12 look most folded with O15 sitting close to N10 and the O-H oriented back toward the ring nitrogen (short N...O, inward H16), giving the best O-H...N bond with little methyl/CH2OH clash. 26, 11 and 25 also place the hydroxyl over the ring near N with acceptable H orientation and only mild H...H crowding. 16, 7, 9, 2, 1, 17, 20, 10, 30 form a middle tier: N...O is borderline (~3.0-3.3 A) or the OH is only partly turned toward N, so any H-bond is weak and compensated by an otherwise unstrained, fairly planar ring. 3, 13, 15, 27, 6, 19 have the arm swung partly away and show some C5/methyl to C12H2 or ring-H crowding and/or noticeable puckering, so they sit lower. The least stable group (29, 8, 14, 4, 18, 22, 24, 23, 21, 28) is clearly extended: O15 is far from N10 (no H-bond), the C9-C12-O15 chain points outward, and several show the ethyl/methyl end eclipsing or brushing the CH2OH/ring hydrogens; 28 and 21 are the most open with the largest N...O separations and added steric exposure, so they are placed last. Uncertainty: exact H-bond strength depends on the H16/N11 directions and on whether N behaves as a good acceptor (enamine) versus poor (amide-like); within the middle tier (roughly ranks 6-22) the differences are subtle (a few kJ/mol) and the order there should be treated as approximate, whereas the folded H-bonded top (5,12,26,11,25) versus the extended bottom (28,21,23,24,22) is the more robust conclusion.

The common framework has a central tertiary-alcohol carbon bearing a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, a two-carbon aldehyde side chain, and a two-carbon terminal-alkyne side chain. Since the molecule is acyclic, there is no ordinary ring strain; the dominant geometric discriminator is formation of a favorable six-membered OH...O=C pseudocycle, followed by weaker OH...alkyne contacts and avoidance of unfavorable gauche or eclipsed arrangements. I used O6-H7 as the principal donor, carbonyl O10 as the strongest acceptor, and the midpoint of C15-C16 as an approximate alkyne-pi acceptor. Six conformers have credible intramolecular OH...O=C hydrogen bonds. Conformer 30 has the shortest and well-directed contact, with H7...O10 about 1.94 Å and an O-H...O angle near 142°. Conformer 10 has a somewhat longer H...O distance, about 2.15 Å, but the best remaining angle, near 139°, plus a secondary propargylic C-H...O contact. Conformers 28 and 17 both have H7...O10 near 2.07 Å and angles around 131-133°; 28 is placed first because its carbonyl and alkyne groups are less folded toward the methyl group. Conformer 20 has a similar hydrogen bond, about 2.11 Å and 132°, together with a weak methyl C-H...O contact, while 23 has the least linear member of this set, about 2.15 Å and 128°. These six are therefore placed before all structures lacking a carbonyl-bound hydroxyl. The next group directs the hydroxyl toward the alkyne. Their H7-to-alkyne-midpoint distances are approximately 2.51 Å for 19, 2.55 Å for 8, 2.60 Å for 7, 2.61 Å for 29, 2.62-2.65 Å for 11, 9, 3, 2, 6, 25, 21 and 27, and about 2.71 Å for 15. The angles are generally only 117-123°, so these are weaker and less directional than the OH...O=C bonds. Conformer 19 combines the shortest OH...pi geometry with a propargylic C-H...O contact near 2.39 Å. Conformer 11 has a slightly longer OH...pi contact but two additional C-H...carbonyl contacts around 2.37 and 2.44 Å. Conformers 8 and 7 have good OH...pi distances and comparatively open alkyne/methyl arrangements. Conformers 3 and 21 are also relatively anti and uncluttered, although their OH...pi distances are slightly longer. Conformers 27 and 29 are close: 27 has a weak methyl C-H...O contact, whereas 29 has the shorter OH...pi distance but a more folded alkyne/methyl relationship. Conformers 6, 2 and 25 have similar OH...pi distances, with minor differences in carbonyl and methyl separation. Conformer 14 lacks OH...pi donation but is promoted by two C-H...carbonyl contacts near 2.38-2.42 Å and an open alkyne/methyl arrangement. Conformer 9 has both OH...pi and C-H...O contacts, but C15 lies only about 2.56 Å from the methyl carbon, indicating a more strained folded torsion. Conformer 15 is open but has the longest meaningful OH...pi approach. The remaining conformers do not present the hydroxyl to either the carbonyl oxygen or the alkyne. Conformer 12 is placed first among them because it retains a weak methyl C-H...O contact near 2.56 Å. Conformer 22 is very extended, with the carbonyl oxygen far from both the hydroxyl and methyl group, minimizing steric compression. Conformers 13, 4, 5, 16, 26 and 1 are also broadly extended; their ordering is based on small differences in carbonyl-to-methyl and alkyne-to-methyl separations and is uncertain. Conformers 24 and especially 18 bring the internal alkyne carbon close to the methyl carbon, approximately 2.65 and 2.58 Å respectively, consistent with a less favorable gauche or partially eclipsed side-chain arrangement; they are therefore placed last. The first six positions are comparatively secure, whereas many spacings after position 7 are likely within about 1-2 kcal/mol and depend on the treatment of weak, nonlinear C-H...O and OH...pi interactions.

I first reconstructed the covalent framework from the short heavy-atom contacts: C2-C3-C6-O9-C10-C2 forms a five-membered cyclic ether, C1 is a methyl substituent on C2, and C10 bears the C11-C13-O15 hydroxyethyl substituent. Thus, for example, C1-C10 distances near 2.5-2.7 A are normal 1,3 relationships rather than clashes. The main differentiators are the tetrahydrofuran-ring pucker, whether the methyl and hydroxyethyl substituents are pseudo-equatorial or pseudo-axial, side-chain gauche/anti relationships, close methyl-side-chain contacts, and especially O15-H16...O9 hydrogen bonding.

Six conformers have a genuine intramolecular alcohol-to-ring-ether hydrogen bond. Their approximate O15...O9 / H16...O9 distances and donor angles are: 3 = 2.785/1.976 A, ca. 30 deg; 5 = 2.786/1.980 A, ca. 30 deg; 12 = 2.786/1.979 A, ca. 27 deg; 23 = 2.814/2.001 A, ca. 28 deg; 17 = 2.773/2.012 A, ca. 34 deg; and 14 = 2.801/2.096 A, ca. 36-38 deg. Conformer 27 has only a weak, bent contact (O...O 3.164 A, H...O 2.576 A, ca. 45 deg). All other conformers have the hydroxyl proton directed away from O9, even when the two oxygen atoms are around 3.6-3.8 A apart.

For the ring, C1...C6 near 3.7 A indicates a more pseudo-equatorial methyl arrangement, whereas about 3.1-3.3 A indicates a more pseudo-axial one. Likewise, C6...C11 near 3.6 A places the hydroxyethyl substituent more pseudo-equatorially, while about 3.0-3.2 A is more pseudo-axial. Conformer 3 combines a strong hydrogen bond with both substituents relatively pseudo-equatorial, making it the clearest minimum. Conformer 23 has a very linear hydrogen bond and an equatorial hydroxyethyl group but a pseudo-axial methyl. Conformer 17 also has the larger side chain pseudo-equatorial and less methyl-side-chain crowding, although its hydrogen bond is slightly less linear and one side-chain closure is tighter. Conformers 5 and 12 have excellent hydrogen bonds but a pseudo-axial hydroxyethyl substituent; 5 has the better methyl orientation, while 12 has the closest methyl-side-chain relationship (C1...C11 about 2.88 A). Conformer 14 has both ring substituents favorably oriented, but its hydrogen bond is the weakest and its pseudo-ring is the tightest, so it is placed last among the hydrogen-bonded set. The order of 23, 17, 5, 12, and 14 is uncertain because hydrogen-bond strength and ring-pucker strain oppose one another.

Among the non-hydrogen-bonded structures, 30 is favored because the larger hydroxyethyl substituent is pseudo-equatorial and the side chain is almost fully anti; its main penalty is the pseudo-axial methyl. Conformer 7 has both ring substituents comparatively well oriented and an anti terminal C-C-O arrangement, but one gauche side-chain torsion. Conformer 8 has an equatorial methyl and extended side chain but a pseudo-axial hydroxyethyl substituent. Conformer 24 keeps both substituents reasonably pseudo-equatorial and has a favorable, weak methyl C-H...O contact around 2.3 A, but retains side-chain gauche strain. Conformers 25 and 1 have equatorial side chains and predominantly extended side-chain geometry, with pseudo-axial methyl groups. Conformers 29, 15, 10, and 6 trade one anti side-chain torsion for another gauche torsion and are separated only subtly.

Conformers 11 and 22 keep the side chain extended but place the larger substituent pseudo-axially; 11 is cleaner sterically, while 22 has closer end-to-end packing. Conformers 16, 13, 19, 9, and 18 combine a pseudo-axial hydroxyethyl group with one or more gauche side-chain torsions. Conformer 28 has the side substituent equatorial but two moderate gauche penalties. The weak hydrogen bond in 27 partly compensates for its folded side chain and pseudo-axial substituent, keeping it above the completely nonbonded, multiply gauche structures. Conformers 4, 2, and 20 have no useful O-H...O bond and several gauche or pseudo-axial penalties. Conformers 26 and 21 are least favorable: both have folded side chains without compensating hydrogen bonding, and 21 additionally has a short methyl-side-chain separation (C1...C11 about 2.89 A), making it the likely highest-energy structure. The middle of the ranking, especially 7/8/24/25, 29/15/10/6, and 16/13/19/9/18, is approximate because the structures represent different trade-offs of comparable ring-pucker and gauche penalties.

I treated the connectivity as fixed: a methyl-bearing stereocenter attached to an aldehyde/formyl carbon and to a CH2-O-CH=NH imidate/formimidate arm. The main geometric handles were therefore (1) whether the imine N can approach the aldehyde carbonyl in a Bürgi-Dunitz-like n_N→π*C=O geometry, (2) whether the N-H points at either oxygen for a true H bond, (3) separation of the two polar ends C=O and O-CH=NH to avoid dipole/donor-acceptor congestion, and (4) methyl versus imidate/aldehyde nonbonded crowding. Most conformers do not have a linear N-H···O aldehyde hydrogen bond; where N is near the carbonyl it is usually the imine lone-pair/carbonyl-carbon contact rather than a clean H bond. Conformers 29, 20, and 12 show a folded geometry with N···C(aldehyde) around 2.1-2.2 Å and approach angles near 100-105°, consistent with strong n→π* interaction/incipient hemiaminal character; I rank them highest, with 12 a little lower because the methyl/imidate crowding is tighter. If those very short N···C contacts are interpreted as purely repulsive rather than attractive, these three would move down, so this is the largest uncertainty. The next group are extended, low-clash arrangements with the methyl group far from the imidate N and the aldehyde and imidate oxygens well separated: 13, 25, 23, 5, 1, 3, 9, 22, 8, 16, 28, 24, 11. Within this group small differences come from O···O/dipole separation and methyl-to-imidate distance rather than any obvious H bond. Middle/lower structures such as 6, 2, 18, 17, 15, 21 have no decisive stabilizing contact and only moderate polar-end separation or mild N/O proximity without good H-bond angle. The least stable structures have short methyl···imidate contacts or crowded polar termini: 30, 14, 26, 7, 19, 4, 10, and especially 27, where the methyl group lies close to the imidate end while no compensating well-oriented N-H···O bond is present.

I first used the alkene carbon pair and its two directly bonded ring atoms as an approximate local plane. In the lower-strain cyclohexene half-chairs, the two remaining saturated ring atoms lie on opposite sides of that plane; structures with both atoms on the same side are boat or twist-boat-like and incur more eclipsing/torsional strain. I then inspected whether the methyl and hydroxymethyl bonds pointed away from the ring or folded over it, together with 1,3-pseudoaxial contacts and hydroxyl orientation. Conformers 24, 3, 29, 21, 25, 15, 16, 8, and 19 form the most favorable half-chair family: both substituents are predominantly pseudo-equatorial. Conformer 24 has the best combination of outward substituent vectors and a clean hydroxymethyl arrangement. Conformers 3, 29, 21, 25, and 15 are very close; they differ mainly by rotation about the ring-CH2OH bond, with one O...ring-carbon contact around 2.91-3.11 A and the other around 3.7-3.8 A. Conformers 16, 8, and 19 place the oxygen gauche to both neighboring ring carbons, giving somewhat greater crowding; 19 also has an approximately 2.1 A hydroxyl-H/ring-H contact. The ordering within this entire top group is uncertain because the differences are mostly small side-chain torsional effects. The second family, 22, 27, 12, 13, 6, 9, 5, and 26, retains a half-chair ring but folds the substituents into more pseudoaxial orientations, producing characteristic 1,3 contacts of roughly 3.1 A. Conformer 22 is placed first in this family because its OH is directed toward the alkene midpoint, with a bent but plausible OH...pi contact of about 2.2 A from the hydroxyl hydrogen; conformer 27 has a similar but longer interaction. Conformers 12, 13, 6, and 9 lack that stabilization but have relatively clean oxygen-to-ring separations. Conformers 5 and 26 have hydroxyl-H/ring-H separations near 2.16-2.18 A and are therefore placed at the bottom of the half-chair-axial group. The remaining conformers 11, 7, 1, 28, 4, 20, 2, 18, 30, 17, 23, 14, and 10 are boat or twist-boat-like, so ring torsional strain is their common penalty. Conformers 11 and 7 are the least crowded members of this family. Conformer 1 has a more twist-like ring and a weak, bent OH...pi arrangement, while 28 and 4 keep their substituents comparatively outward. Conformers 20, 2, and 18 receive small OH...pi benefits but remain boat-like. Conformers 30, 17, and 23 have no comparably useful polar contact; 23 also has a hydroxyl-H/ring-H distance near 2.06 A. Conformers 14 and 10 are ranked last because they combine the high-energy boat framework with a more pseudoaxial methyl group, with 10 showing the slightly less favorable hydroxymethyl placement. Overall, the three-family separation is more reliable than the fine ordering within each family, where several structures are likely separated by less than the uncertainty of a purely geometric estimate.

I treated the common skeleton as CH3-CH(CH2OH)-CH2-CH2-NH-CHO and compared the same atom mapping in every block: amide N-H, formyl C=O, alcohol O-H, the stereocenter bearing methyl and hydroxymethyl, and the two methylene linkers. The dominant geometric discriminator is intramolecular hydrogen bonding. The best motifs are short, nearly linear O-H...O=C contacts and six-membered N-H...O alcohol closures; I used donor-H...acceptor distance, heavy D...A distance, approximate directionality, and whether the chain looked folded into a favorable ring rather than merely bringing methyl groups near the amide. Conformers 7 and 23 have the shortest and most linear alcohol-to-carbonyl hydrogen bonds, with O...O around 2.81-2.83 A and H...O around 1.87-1.91 A, so they are placed highest. Conformer 10 has a very good six-membered N-H...O alcohol closure, N...O about 2.82 A and H...O about 1.91 A with reasonable directionality; 6 and 24 are similar but slightly less favorable in angle or peripheral steric layout. Conformers 14, 8, 21, and 30 also show strong O-H...O=C hydrogen bonds, with somewhat longer O...O distances than 7/23 or slightly less ideal chain geometry. Conformers 4 and 9 still have clear O-H...O=C contacts, but the O...O separation is closer to 2.95 A, so they rank below the strongest set. Conformers 25, 15, 5, and 1 have only moderate or directional imperfect hydrogen bonds: 25 and 15 are N-H...O closures with H...O near 2.02-2.03 A but not ideal linearity, while 5 and 1 have longer O-H...O=C contacts and 1 additionally looks more folded with methyl nearer the amide region. Conformers 18 and 19 show H...O separations around 2.17 A but poor N-H...O angles, so I count them as weak at best. Conformers 2 and 22 have only marginal long contacts. The remaining structures lack a convincing intramolecular hydrogen bond; among them I favored more extended arrangements with fewer methyl-to-amide or methyl-to-carbonyl proximities, and penalized compact conformers such as 27, 28, 11, 13, 16, and 3 where the methyl branch is closer to the polar terminus or the chain appears more gauche without a compensating hydrogen bond. Because no energies or vibrational/entropic terms are available and many differences are within a few tenths of an angstrom, the ordering inside the strong-hydrogen-bond group and inside the no-hydrogen-bond tail is uncertain, but the broad trend is robust: geometries with a short linear O-H...O=C or well-formed six-membered N-H...O contact are most stable, weak or angular contacts are intermediate, and extended but contact-free or compact sterically pressured conformers are least stable.

Connectivity (fixed for all): a central stereocarbon (C5) bearing a methyl (C1), a hydroxymethyl arm (C6-O7H8) and a carbinol carbon (C12-O20H21); C12 is attached to an aziridine ring (N15H16-C14H2-C13H). Because connectivity and the strained 3-membered ring are identical in every block, relative stability is governed by (a) intramolecular H-bonds among the two OH groups and the aziridine N, (b) whether the OH protons actually point at the acceptor (H...A distance and D-H...A angle), and (c) absence of short nonbonded contacts (extended = clash-free but H-bond-poor). I estimated donor/acceptor geometry from the coordinates for O7-H8, O20-H21, N15-H16.

A clear intramolecular O-H...O bond (O...O ~2.77-2.82 A, H...O ~1.93-2.08 A, angle >~135 deg) is the dominant stabilizer, worth several kcal/mol, and chelation of O20 by the aziridine N (O20...N ~2.8 A with N-H...O or O-H...N contact) adds further stabilization. Conformer 12 has the shortest, most linear O20-H21...O7 bond (H...O ~1.93 A, ~143 deg) plus O20...N ~2.77 A and N-H...O20 ~2.31 A. Conformer 1 is similar (1.96 A/140 deg with N...O20 2.78 A and NH...O20 2.32 A). Conformer 30 shows the densest contact set (OH...O ~2.04 A, O20...N 2.78 A, O20-H...N ~2.77 A, NH...O20 ~2.30 A). Conformer 9 is unique in a cooperative relay O20-H...O7-H...N (O7-H8...N15 ~2.32 A, 143 deg) while still keeping O20...N ~2.77 A. Conformers 13, 2 and 4 combine a good OH...O (~1.95-2.07 A) with O20...N ~2.8-2.9 A and an NH...O contact; 22 has the same chelation around O20/N but its OH...O is more bent (~134 deg), so it sits just behind.

The next group has one strong, fairly linear OH...O bond but little/no N engagement: 6 (1.96 A/142 deg), 21 (1.96 A/140 deg, plus O20...N 2.92 A), 10 (1.96 A/142 deg), 16 (1.98 A/140 deg), 20 (1.98 A/139 deg), 7 (2.01 A/140 deg), 11 (2.01 A/137 deg with O20...N 3.06 A). Differences among these are small (a few tenths of an Angstrom / a few degrees) and ordering here is uncertain. Then come conformers whose OH...O is present but bent/weaker: 14 (2.03 A/135 deg), 24 (2.02 A/133 deg, somewhat bifurcated), 29 (2.06 A/131 deg), 27 (2.08 A/128 deg, clearly strained).

Below that the two OH groups are too far apart for a real bond (O...O 3.0-3.8 A) and stability rests only on weak O20...N proximity: 18 (O20...N 2.77 A but N-H...O angle ~105 deg, poor), 5 (O20...N 2.78 A, NH...O bent ~105 deg), 15 (O...O 3.02 A, H...O 2.40 A and only ~122 deg). The most extended, essentially H-bond-free conformers (O...O >3.6 A, only weak O20...N ~3.0-3.2 A) are least stable: 23, 8, 25, 3, 26, 28, 17, and finally 19, which is the most extended (O7...O20 ~4.9 A) with no compensating interaction. Extended geometries avoid clashes, but the lost H-bond energy outweighs the modest steric relief, so they occupy the bottom. Uncertainty is largest within the single-strong-H-bond block (roughly ranks 9-17) and among the bent/weak mid-tier (14-19).

The molecule is 4-hydroxybutyl ethanimidate: CH3-C(=NH)-O-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-OH (22 atoms, same connectivity in all blocks). The dominant stabilizing factor is an intramolecular O-H···O(ester) hydrogen bond closing a favorable 6-membered pseudoring (O5-C6-C7-C8-C9-O10), with a possible secondary N-H···O or O-H···N interaction. I measured key distances for each conformer. STRONG H-BOND GROUP (most stable): Conformer 3 has the best H-bond (H···O ~1.87 Å, O···O 2.79 Å, nearly linear ~159°); 18 (~1.90 Å, 154°) and 20 (~1.91 Å, 153°) are essentially tied next; 2 (~2.02 Å, 154°) is good; 12 (~2.09 Å, ~139°) and 13 (~2.22 Å, ~138°) are progressively weaker but genuine. WEAK/MARGINAL GROUP: 14 shows a short N···O contact (3.17 Å) with both N-H and O-H oriented toward each other (weak bifurcated N-H···O / O-H···N, angles ~115-130°); 21 has a very weak O-H···O contact (H···O ~2.78 Å, angle ~118°) — barely stabilizing. NO-H-BOND GROUP: all remaining conformers have O5···O10 > 4.2 Å or the OH pointing away from the ester O, so they lack the ~3-5 kcal/mol H-bond stabilization. Within this group I ranked more extended (all-trans-like) chains higher, since they minimize gauche/eclipsing strain: 23 (O···O 6.2 Å, fully extended), 17, 10, 16, 24, 8, 28, 15, 22, 26 are extended; 19, 27, 25, 11, 29, 9, 30, 4, 7 are medium-folded (O···O 4.3-4.6 Å) with some gauche penalties; 6, 5, 1 are compact WITHOUT an H-bond (O···O 3.4-3.5 Å with the OH hydrogen pointing away from the ester oxygen), which combines folding strain with unfavorable dipole/lone-pair alignment of the two oxygens — these are the least stable, with 1 worst (closest nonbonded O···O approach, 3.42 Å). The C=NH unit is Z (N-H away from methyl) in all conformers, so it is not a discriminator, and no conformer shows severe (<2.2 Å) H···H steric clashes. UNCERTAINTY: (a) ordering within the strong H-bond group (3/18/20 nearly degenerate); (b) the mid-field of extended no-H-bond conformers (9th-27th places) where only subtle gauche/torsional differences distinguish them — this portion of the ranking is low-confidence; (c) the weak H-bonds in 14 and 21 could be worth anywhere from 0.5-2 kcal/mol, so their placement near the top of the no-H-bond pack is approximate.

I treated the connectivity as N≡C-CH2-O-CH2-CH2-cyclopropyl: the nitrile/ether termini are polar but there are no X-H donors, so no conventional intramolecular H-bond is possible; N...O is nearly constant (~3.4 A) because of the short N-C-C-O linkage and was not a useful discriminator. Cyclopropane ring strain is essentially invariant, so ranking was based on rotatable-bond geometry. I used three 1-4 probes as torsion/strain diagnostics: C2...C5 for C2-C3-O-C5, C3...C6 for C3-O-C5-C6, and O4...C7 for O-C5-C6-C7, plus the N-to-cyclopropyl end-to-end distance. Values >~3.5-3.7 A indicate anti/open arrangements; ~3.0-3.2 A are gauche; <~3.0 A are close 1-4 contacts. Conformers 27 and 2 are the most convincing minima: all three probes are anti (~3.61-3.73 A) and the chain is maximally extended (~8.2 A to the far ring carbon), with 27 slightly more symmetrically extended. 12, 29, and 9 keep the nitrile-ether and ether-alkyl probes open but retain one gauche/close C3...C6 contact near the cyclopropyl, so they follow; 12 and 29 are a little more extended than 9. 23, 17, and 30 each have two good anti probes but one residual contact (O...cyclopropyl for 23; nitrile-side C2...C5 for 17/30), with 17/30 ordered by extension. The middle set (26,5,4,6,10,24,16,19,28,25,8,15) combines one good anti segment with one or two gauche/close contacts; I favored structures that keep the central C3-O-C5-C6 backbone open and avoid <2.95 A O...C/C...C contacts, using larger end-to-end distance as a tie-breaker. The least stable group is either compact (short N-to-ring distance) or simultaneously gauche at all three probes: 21,7,22,14,13 are folded with several ~3.0-3.2 A contacts; 11,1,3,18 are extended in space but locally helical/gauche at C2...C5, C3...C6, and O...C7; 20 is placed last because it combines a very short C2...C5 contact (~2.88 A), a gauche C3...C6, and a compact N-to-cyclopropyl distance. Uncertainty is high within neighboring pairs, especially 27/2, 12/29/9, and the broad middle tier; including explicit dispersion or a different dipole convention could swap adjacent labels, but the overall anti/open versus gauche/compact trend should be robust.

I treated the connectivity as a seven-membered oxepene-like ring with an endocyclic C4=C5 double bond, an ether oxygen in the ring (O11), and a hydroxymethyl substituent at C4 (C3-O1-H2). First I checked for an intramolecular O1-H...O11 hydrogen bond: none is a strong linear H-bond, because the closest O1...O11 separations are still about 3.55-3.65 A (conformers 7, 23, 28, 6). Among these, 23 has the best O-H vector toward O11 and a relatively open chair/twist-chair ring; 28 and 6 look fairly balanced; 7 has the shortest O...O distance but shows somewhat tighter transannular C4...C10/C6...C10 contacts, so I placed it just after the cleaner near-contact cases. Next I favored structures that keep C4 approximately trigonal planar for the C4=C5 alkene, avoid twisting the double bond, keep the C3 hydroxymethyl group pseudo-outside rather than folded across the ring, and avoid inward-pointing C12/C10 methylene hydrogens. The extended conformers 4, 14, 30, 10, and 12 do not gain H-bond stabilization, but they also avoid severe transannular crowding and keep the alkene reasonably planar, so they occupy the upper-middle. The broad middle (8, 18, 20, 22, 25, 29, 24, 27, 13, 19, 9, 3, 5, 2, 21, 17) is genuinely uncertain: differences are mostly subtle ring-pucker/torsion changes rather than obvious clashes, and small force-field choices could reorder several neighbors. I ranked lowest the conformers with O1 and O11 far apart while the OH points away or only perpendicular to the acceptor (1, 16, 11, 15, 26), especially 26 and 15 where the hydroxyl is most isolated from the ring ether and the ring still has medium-ring eclipsing/transannular strain. The ordering within the middle third should be considered approximate; the clearest distinctions are the favorable near-contact/weak-H-bond group at the top and the non-interacting, more strained/extended group at the bottom.

Step 1 - Connectivity/formula. Each block has 7 C, 12 H, 2 O (C7H12O2, two degrees of unsaturation). Tracing bond distances (e.g. in conf 12) gives a fixed bicyclic core: atoms C5-C7-C9-O12-C13-C15 form an oxane ring, but an extra C7-C13 bond (~1.54 A) closes it into a 2-oxabicyclo[2.2.0]hexane (fused oxetane + cyclobutane) that carries a -CH2-CH2-OH (2-hydroxyethyl) substituent at C5. Because connectivity is identical, the large bicyclic ring strain is essentially constant across all 30 and is NOT a discriminator. What varies is (i) the side-chain torsion C5-C4-C3-O1 (anti/extended vs gauche/folded), (ii) rotation about C3-O1 that can aim the OH at the ring ether oxygen O12, and (iii) resulting steric/dipolar contacts of the chain with the strained core.

Step 2 - Intramolecular H-bond screen (dominant term). For each conformer I computed the hydroxyl O1...O12(ether) distance and the H2...O12 distance/angle. Only two structures give a genuine short, near-linear O-H...O bond: conf 30 (O...O 2.94 A, H...O 2.00 A, O-H...O ~164 deg) and conf 15 (O...O 2.95 A, H...O 2.05 A, ~153 deg). These gain several kcal/mol and must sit at the top; 30 is slightly more linear/shorter than 15, so 30 > 15. All other conformers have O1...O12 >= ~3.8 A (most 4.4-6.0 A), i.e. no H-bond.

Step 3 - Ranking the 28 non-H-bonded conformers. With no H-bond available, stability is governed by side-chain torsion and steric compression. An extended/anti hydroxyethyl chain moves O1 far from the bicyclic core (large O1...O12 ~5.7-6.0 A), minimizing 1,5-H...H clashes and O(lone-pair)/core dipole repulsion -> lower energy. Folded/gauche chains bring O1 back toward the core (O1...O12 ~3.8-4.4 A) without any H-bond payoff, so they pay steric/dipolar cost -> higher energy. I therefore ordered the non-H-bonded set essentially by increasing extension (decreasing fold), using O1...O12 as a compactness proxy: most extended 24(5.99),3(5.98),20(5.94),11(5.89),1(5.85),14(5.80),10/12(5.70),21(5.68),9(5.66),19(5.63); mid/gauche-but-open 29(5.44),23(5.28),6(5.27),28(5.22),5(5.06),7(5.03),26(5.02),4(4.87),27(4.71),8(4.66); clearly folded with O1 near the core but OH not engaged 13(4.44),22(4.40),25(4.28),17(4.11),2(3.90),18(3.90),16(3.85) -> least stable, with 16 worst (shortest O...O and the OH hydrogen pointed away, so only repulsion).

Step 4 - Uncertainty. The top two (30,15) and the bottom folded cluster (16,18,2,17,25) are fairly secure. The broad middle (roughly ranks 3-25) is uncertain: O1...O12 is only a proxy and I cannot resolve individual torsional eclipsing or subtle H...H clashes for every structure by hand, so adjacent entries there could easily swap. The intrinsic (and large) bicyclic strain is common to all and was excluded from the ordering.

All 30 blocks are the same C6H12O2 scaffold: a puckered cyclobutane ring (C5-C7-C10-C13) bearing a hydroxyethyl substituent (C3-C4-O1H) on C5 and a hydroxyl (O11H) on C10 (1,3 across the ring). Connectivity and the cyclobutane ring strain are common to every conformer, so relative stability is governed mainly by (a) intramolecular H-bonding between the two OH groups, (b) dipole/lone-pair repulsion when the oxygens are close but NOT H-bonded, (c) folded vs extended hydroxyethyl chain (gauche/anti about C3-C4-C5) and (d) OH dipole alignment/close contacts. I computed the O1...O11 separation and the O-H...O geometry for each.

A clear intramolecular H-bond (O...O 2.87-2.92 A with near-linear O-H...O) is present in only four conformers: 25 (2.87 A, H...O 1.91 A, angle ~170 deg), 19 (2.88 A, H...O 1.92 A, ~170 deg), 30 (2.89 A, H...O 1.94 A, ~163 deg) and 11 (2.92 A, H...O 1.99 A, ~160 deg). This ~3-5 kcal/mol stabilization outweighs the modest folding strain, so these four are the most stable; 25/19 are slightly better (shorter O...O, more linear) than 30/11.

At the opposite extreme, conformers 15 (O...O 3.85 A), 23 (4.05 A) and 5 (4.26 A) bring the two oxygens close enough for strong dipole/lone-pair repulsion yet too far for a real H-bond, while simultaneously requiring a folded (gauche) hydroxyethyl chain - stabilization with no payoff. These are the least stable, with 15 (closest non-bonded O...O, most folded) the worst, then 23, then 5.

The remaining 23 are non-H-bonded and rank mainly by how extended/anti the chain is (larger O...O = opposed OH dipoles, staggered, fewer folded gauche penalties) versus partially folded intermediate geometries. Very extended anti conformers (O...O ~6.4-6.6 A: 9,18,14,10,22,21) are the best of the non-bonded set; moderately extended (~6.1-6.3 A: 7,27,1,6,17,16,28,4) follow; intermediate folded geometries (5.0-5.7 A: 20,2,29,26,24,3,12,13,8) incur growing gauche/dipole costs as O...O shrinks, with 8 (5.06) and 13 (5.16) the worst of this tier, just above the 5/23/15 group.

Uncertainty: within the extended tier (roughly ranks 5-18) differences are <~1 kcal/mol and depend on subtle cyclobutane pucker and OH torsions that I can only estimate from coordinates, so that internal order is approximate; the robust conclusions are the H-bonded top-4 (25,19,30,11) and the repulsive, folded non-bonded bottom-3 (5,23,15 with 15 last).

The connectivity is the same in every block: an aldehyde terminus (O1-C2H), a two-carbon methylene linker (C3-C6), a rigid C7≡C8 alkyne, and a C9-C10-N11 aziridine ring. Because the aziridine ring and alkyne are present in all conformers, the discriminating terms are rotations about C2-C3, C3-C6 and C8-C9: extended/anti arrangements separate the carbonyl and aziridine termini and minimize allylic/1,3-steric crowding, whereas gauche or folded arrangements bring O1/C2/C3 toward C9/C10/N11. I checked especially O1...N11 and O1...H12 for a possible intramolecular N-H...O=C hydrogen bond, but none is a clean short contact: the closest carbonyl-to-N-H approaches are still only weak/long (about 3.6-3.9 A for H12...O1 in 6 and 28, with O...N around 4.5-4.7 A), so I treated them as at most weak electrostatic compensation, not true H bonds. Conformers with very large end-to-end separation and nearly anti aldehyde-linker-alkyne geometry (14, 4, 22, 16, 12, 13, 15, 7, 23, 30, 29) are therefore favored. Moderately extended but visibly bent structures (26, 19, 2, 25, 3, 27, 9, 24, 21) follow; their ranking is uncertain because local C2-C3/C3-C6 torsions cannot be judged exactly without energies. More compact structures (18, 5, 17, 10, 8, 20) lose stability through increased gauche crowding but show no obvious sub-2 A H...H crash. The least favored are the most folded cases: 6 and 28 have the carbonyl and aziridine termini closest and may gain only weak dipole/N-H...O attraction; 11 and especially 1 are folded without a compensating H-bond geometry, leaving steric/eclipsing penalties uncompensated.
